main.title: Compact disc
main.summary: The compact disc (CD) is a digital optical disc data storage format co-developed by Philips and Sony to store and play digital audio recordings.

cards.heading: Compact disc
cards.text:
The compact disc (CD) is a digital optical disc data storage format co-developed by Philips and Sony to store and play digital audio recordings. It employs the Compact Disc Digital Audio (CD-DA) standard and is capable of holding uncompressed stereo audio. First released in Japan in October 1982, the CD was the second optical disc format to reach the market, following the larger LaserDisc (LD). In later years, the technology was adapted for computer data storage as CD-ROM and subsequently expanded into various writable and multimedia formats. By 2007, over 200 billion CDs (including audio CDs, CD-ROMs, and CD-Rs) had been sold worldwide.

Standard CDs have a diameter of 120 mm (4.7 in) and typically hold up to 74 minutes of audio or approximately 650 MiB (681,574,400 bytes) of data. This was later regularly extended to 80 minutes or 700 MiB (734,003,200 bytes) by reducing the spacing between data tracks, with some discs unofficially reaching up to 99 minutes or 870 MiB (912,261,120 bytes) which falls outside established specifications.

main.title: Falklands War
main.summary: Argentina invaded the Falkland Islands on 2 April 1982 and South Georgia the following day.

cards.heading: Falklands War
cards.text: Argentina invaded the Falkland Islands on 2 April 1982 and South Georgia the following day. Britain sent a naval task force on 5 April to retake the territories, beginning a ten-week war in the South Atlantic. The fighting ended with the Argentine surrender on 14 June. It killed 649 Argentine and 255 British military personnel, along with three islanders. Argentina regarded its action as reclaiming disputed territory; Britain regarded it as an invasion of its colony. The military outcome restored British control while leaving the sovereignty dispute unresolved.

main.title: Thriller
main.summary: Michael Jackson released Thriller on 29 November 1982, working again with producer Quincy Jones after Off the Wall.

cards.heading: Thriller
cards.text: Michael Jackson released Thriller on 29 November 1982, working again with producer Quincy Jones after Off the Wall. Recorded at Westlake Studios in Los Angeles, the album brings together post-disco, synth-pop, funk and rock, with songs about romance, paranoia and social concerns. Billie Jean and Beat It reached number one in the United States. Five more singles entered the Top 10, setting a record for one album. Thriller itself spent 37 non-consecutive weeks at the top of the American album chart, carrying the record's varied sound to an unusually large audience.

main.title: Tron
main.summary: Tron brought a programmer into a computer's software world in 1982.

cards.heading: Tron
cards.text: Tron brought a programmer into a computer's software world in 1982. Jeff Bridges plays Kevin Flynn, who meets personified programs while trying to escape the mainframe. Writer-director Steven Lisberger had begun developing the idea after encountering Pong in 1976. What started as an animation project eventually combined live actors, backlit animation and extensive computer-generated imagery. Disney financed the film after other studios rejected it. Its production brought the visual language of computing and video games into a feature film, making the digital environment both the setting and a major technical undertaking.

main.title: ZX Spectrum
main.summary: The ZX Spectrum is an 8-bit home computer developed and marketed by Sinclair Research, first released in Britain on April 23, 1982.

cards.heading: ZX Spectrum
cards.text:
The ZX Spectrum is an 8-bit home computer developed and marketed by Sinclair Research. First released in Britain on April 23, 1982, it became one of the best-selling British computers, with more than five million units sold, and an important platform for home computing and games.

Clive Sinclair's small Cambridge team designed it to use few components and keep costs low. Timex manufactured the machine in Dundee, Scotland. Rick Dickinson designed its case, rainbow motif and rubber keyboard, while the Spectrum name highlighted its colour display. Users connected it to a television and loaded or saved software on compact audio cassettes.

main.title: MIDI
main.summary: MIDI connects electronic instruments and computers through messages describing notes and performance controls.

cards.heading: MIDI
cards.text:
MIDI, the Musical Instrument Digital Interface, is a standard connecting electronic musical instruments, computers and related devices. Pressing a key or moving a knob produces an event containing instructions such as pitch, timing or velocity. A connected sound module uses those instructions to generate the sound.

A single MIDI cable can carry sixteen channels, each routed to a different device. A keyboard can therefore control an external synthesiser, while a sequencer or digital audio workstation records the performance for editing and playback. MIDI messages travel through dedicated MIDI connections or USB.

main.title: DynaTAC
main.summary: The DynaTAC is a series of cellular telephones manufactured by Motorola from 1983 to 1994.

cards.heading: DynaTAC
cards.text:
The DynaTAC is a series of cellular telephones manufactured by Motorola from 1983 to 1994. Unveiled on March 6, 1983, the DynaTAC was the first commercially available handheld cellular phone. A full charge took roughly 10 hours, and it offered 30 minutes of talk time. It also offered an LED display for dialing or recall of one of 30 phone numbers. It was priced at US$3,995 in 1984, its commercial release year, equivalent to $12,804.76 in 2025.

Several models followed, starting in 1985 with the 8000s and continuing with periodic updates of increasing frequency until 1993's Classic II. The DynaTAC was replaced in most roles by the much smaller MicroTAC when it was first introduced in 1989, and by the time of the StarTAC's release in 1996, it was obsolete.

main.title: THX
main.summary: Developed at Lucasfilm in 1983, THX established reproduction standards intended to let cinema audiences hear a film's soundtrack as intended.

cards.heading: THX
cards.text:
THX Ltd. is an American audio company based in the San Francisco Bay Area, known for its suite of digital high fidelity audiovisual reproduction standards for movie theaters, screening rooms, home theaters, computer speakers, car audio systems, video game consoles, and video games. The THX trailer that precedes compliant films is based on the Deep Note, with a distinctive glissando up from a rumbling low pitch.

THX was developed by Tomlinson Holman at George Lucas's company Lucasfilm in 1983 to ensure that the soundtrack for the third Star Wars film, Return of the Jedi, would be accurately reproduced in the best venues. THX was named after Holman's initials, with the "X" standing for "crossover" or "experiment". The name is also an homage to Lucas's first film, THX 1138 (1971). Deep Note was created by Holman's co-worker James A. Moorer.

main.title: Tokyo Disneyland opens
main.subtitle: Disney’s first park outside the United States
main.summary: Tokyo Disneyland opened in Urayasu, Chiba, on 15 April 1983, becoming the first Disney theme park outside the United States.

cards.heading: Disney’s first park outside the United States
cards.text: Tokyo Disneyland opened on a rainy April 15, 1983, in Urayasu, Chiba, beside Tokyo Bay. Developed by Oriental Land through an agreement with Disney, it became the first Disney theme park outside the United States. Construction lasted two years and four months, followed by training and preview visits. President Masatomo Takahashi welcomed the first guests in World Bazaar. The park brought Disney's themed streets, attractions and hospitality to Japan, becoming an important reference for later international expansion.

main.title: Dragon Ball
main.summary: Akira Toriyama's Dragon Ball began serialisation in Weekly Shōnen Jump in 1984.

cards.heading: Dragon Ball
cards.text: Akira Toriyama's Dragon Ball began serialisation in Weekly Shōnen Jump in 1984. Young Son Goku travels in search of seven magical orbs that together summon a dragon able to grant a wish. Martial-arts training, new friendships and battles carry him from childhood into adulthood. Toriyama drew on Journey to the West and Hong Kong martial-arts films, gradually shifting the manga's balance from comedy towards fighting action. Its 519 chapters ran until 1995 and filled 42 collected volumes. Toei's television adaptations extended the story's audience through Dragon Ball and Dragon Ball Z.
